findings.title: Field validity reads the record's self-declared summary and a component envelope
findings.description: FieldRangeCondition and FieldFiniteCondition decide from FieldRecord.summary (minimum, maximum, non_finite). FieldRecord checks the summary's internal consistency but never binds it to the bytes its ScientificDataReference names. A record whose summary says [300, 310] K reports IN_DOMAIN against a 400 K bound, whatever the referenced values are. For a multi-component field the envelope is taken over flattened components: a 3-component velocity (1, 1, 1) m/s, with |u| = 1.732, is IN_DOMAIN against a 1.2 m/s maximum. The docstring says 'the whole represented field envelope', and nothing tells a declarer that the bound applies per component, not to the magnitude. No production domain uses these conditions yet.
findings.evidence: structured_validity.py:128-155 (reads value.summary only), 214-221. fields/result.py:39-73 (FieldSummary not bound to data), 174-176 (is_finite from the summary count). data/field.py:166-175 (summary computed over flattened components). Output of r6_struct_diag.py S1: 'status for a record whose bytes are never read: in_domain' / '3-component field with |u|=1.732 against maximum 1.2 m/s: in_domain'.
findings.reproduction: r6_struct_diag.py section S1.
findings.fix_direction: Bind the summary to the content digest: compute it when the reference is resolved, or record the summary's digest with the reference and verify it on resolution. Make component semantics explicit: refuse FieldRangeCondition on components > 1 unless the declaration says component-wise or magnitude.

verification.reason:
I reproduced both behaviours against src.

1. **The summary is never checked against the stored data.** In `structured_validity.py` (lines 128-155 and 214-221), both conditions read only `FieldRecord.summary`. `FieldRecord.__post_init__` checks the reference's count against the shape and its unit against the definition, but never compares the summary to the data the reference names. `FieldRecord.from_dict` accepts any summary. `FieldValue.from_record` loads the real values and never compares them to the summary either.
   - A record that reuses the reference to real 400-408 K data, with a summary claiming 300-310 K, gets IN_DOMAIN against a 350 K maximum, both directly and through `ValidityDomain.assess`.
   - A doctored `from_dict` payload gets IN_DOMAIN the same way.

2. **Multi-component fields are bounded per component.** `FieldValue.summary()` (`data/field.py:166-175`) flattens all components, so a vector field is bounded component by component, not by magnitude. A (1,1,1) m/s velocity, whose magnitude is 1.732, gets IN_DOMAIN against a 1.2 m/s maximum.

Why only P3:
- The normal production route, `FieldValue.store`, always computes the summary from the real values, so a false summary needs a hand-built or deserialized record.
- Any validity context value is already stated by the caller unless a domain reserves it as derived. A bare Quantity in a `RangeCondition` is no more tied to real data, so the gap is mostly that a content-addressed reference looks like a binding when it isn't.
- The module docstring (lines 8-10) says conditions check the flat component representation, which partly warns about the per-component bound. Nothing warns that the bound is not a magnitude bound.
- No code under src/ or benchmarks/ declares `FieldRangeCondition` or `FieldFiniteCondition`.

The audit document does not mention it, so it is new. This is hardening, not a reachable path to unjustified confidence.

findings.title: A validity domain is a box of point checks: joint regions and input uncertainty cannot be stated
findings.description: Every condition is evaluated independently on one point value (_within compares a scalar magnitude; Quantity has no uncertainty). The only relation between inputs is CrossLimitCondition, a ratio of two declared names. A model whose evidence covers a correlated or non-rectangular region reports IN_DOMAIN at corners of the box that no data support, and an input whose uncertainty straddles a bound is IN_DOMAIN at its nominal value. The audit states the same box limitation for predictive UQ (CORE-006 residual). ValidityDomain, which every domain verdict passes through, has the same limitation, and nothing in an assessment says its region is a box.

So a domain declared as T in [250, 350] K and P in [1, 10] bar reports (350 K, 1 bar) as `in_domain`. That is exactly what the declaration says.

2. Joint regions can be stated. `ValidityDomain` has a channel built for this: `derived_quantities` plus `assembled=` (definition.py:1307-1343 and `_merge` at 1510-1559). A domain's assembler can compute any scalar or flag from several inputs, such as a hull-membership flag, an offset from a diagonal band, or a dimensionless group, and bind a `RangeCondition` or `FlagCondition` to it. A caller cannot forge that value; `_merge` refuses a reserved name in declared input. Domains already do this: the Biot number in thermal_models/lumped.py, C-rate utilization and the capacity-temperature drift ratio in battery/models.py, and the utilization ratios in electrical/dc_applicability.py. Each of these is a non-rectangular region in the input space. My run shows the same corner refused as `outside_validated_domain` once the domain states the joint region.

3. Input uncertainty. It is true that `Quantity` carries no uncertainty, so a nominal value just inside a bound whose uncertainty crosses it is `in_domain`. But this is documented as exact applicability logic (the `RangeCondition` docstring), and a domain can still assemble a worst-case bound, such as the upper end of T, through the same derived channel.

What is left is a missing convenience and an unstated assumption. There is no built-in joint or uncertain region type, and an assessment does not say its region is a box. That is P3 hardening, not a path where the core overstates evidence. Whether a box matches what the evidence covers is the declaring domain's call, which is out of scope here.

The finding is real, but I rate it P2, not P1.

Code facts, from the implementation:
- **The guard keys by region id, not by edge.** In `require_complete_boundary` (conditions.py:326-356), `by_id`, the `seen` duplicate check and the `missing` completeness check all use `region_id`. - **The solver silently picks a winner.** `SteadyConductionProblem.edges` (conduction2d.py:215-222) is a dict built edge by edge, so the last condition wins. The assembly (473, 499-512), `_worst_dirichlet_error` (759) and the provenance `boundary_laws` (370, 723) all read `problem.edges`. The losing condition is never imposed and never checked.
- **Which condition wins depends only on the order of the conditions.** Dirichlet then Neumann gives T:max 300 K; the same two in reverse give T:max 400 K. Both runs report all three checks as PASS. This is the "iteration order deciding a boundary value" defect that the module docstring and `_require_corners_agree` say they refuse.
- **It is new.** The audit doc has no mention of it.

Why P2 and not P1:
- **It is not a normal path.** It needs a hand-built `regions` tuple with a second `MeshRegion` on an edge, plus a contradictory condition on it. The default regions (`boundary_regions`, `plate_problem`) cannot produce this. `SteadyConductionProblem` has no serialization and no MCP or case JSON route, and the only non-test callers are benchmark audit scripts.
- **The result does not misreport what was solved.** `boundary_laws` truthfully records the law that ran. The mismatch is between the input declaration and the output.
- **The passing checks award nothing.** All carry `establishes=None`, and conduction2d is deliberately left out of the threshold registry, so no level is ever granted.
- **The subset-of-regions case fails loudly.** The guard accepts it, but the solve raises a KeyError instead of returning a result. That is a P3 refusal-quality issue, not silent confidence.

I could not refute this. It is confirmed in the code and by running it, and it is new: the audit doc says nothing about corners, and CORE-018 only fixed consensus and bound ordering.

**How the defect arises**
- `_require_corners_agree` (conditions.py:398-404) compares the raw floats from `first.law.evaluate` and `other.law.evaluate`.
- `SpatialProfile.evaluate` returns the magnitude in the law's own unit. For a constant law, `ConstantProfile.evaluate` (profiles.py:236) returns `value.magnitude` with no conversion.
- The only unit check on a Dirichlet value is `require_output_dimension` (conditions.py:175). It compares dimensionality only, so kelvin, degC and millikelvin all pass as [temperature].
- Nothing before the corner check converts to `definition.unit`. The error message then prints both numbers with `definition.unit`, so it misreports 26.85 degC as "26.85 kelvin".

**Not limited to offset units**
Any change of scale within one dimension breaks the guard:
- 300 K against 300 mK is accepted.
- 300 K against 300000 mK is refused.
- 5 V against 5000 mV is refused.

**Reachable through the domain**
`SteadyConductionProblem` accepts the conflicting problem. The assembly converts each edge to the field unit (`evaluate_on_region(..., unit=field.unit)`), and the edge written last, bottom/top, sets every corner to 573.15 K.

**Mitigation, which is why this stays P2 rather than P1**
In conduction2d, the domain's own `boundary_conditions_held` check reports FAIL on the wrongly accepted case, so that one consumer does not show unjustified confidence. What remains:
- The generic core guard is silently wrong in both directions.
- Any other consumer that relies on it gets no protection.
- Problems that are physically consistent (300 K with 26.85 degC, or K with mK) are refused, with a misleading unit label.

Writing every edge in the field's unit works around it. That fits P2: a significant limitation that silently weakens a guard.

findings.title: Transfer records bind neither their source record nor their instant order: stale and final crossings coexist, and the canonical order lets the stale one win
findings.description: QuantityTransfer requires source_record_id and instant to be non-empty but checks neither against anything. There is no API to verify the value against the named result, and a transfer naming "any-string-at-all" carrying 999 K constructs. In production, ambient_transfers names the thermal result_id while taking the value from system configuration; ambient is a CONTROL input of the thermal problem, not a value in that result. require_agreeing_transfers keys on the instant string, so transfers of one dependency at different instants (a stale iteration 9 and the final iteration 10) coexist in one ProvenanceRecord without refusal. It sorts them lexicographically by that key, which places 'coupled_iteration:9' after 'coupled_iteration:10'. mcp/problem._ambient_by_component keeps the last transfer per component, so it would select the stale 400 K over the final 300 K. The current in-process writer records only the final iteration, which keeps this latent.
findings.evidence: transfer.py:113-122 (non-empty checks only) and 316 (`sorted(seen.values(), key=lambda t: t.key)` where key ends in the instant string). mcp/problem.py:1754-1772 (last one wins per component). systems/electrothermal/coupled.py:1086-1098 (the value is `stage.body.ambient_temperature`, the source_record_id is `source.result_id`). r10_instants.py printed: "provenance.transfers order: ['coupled_iteration:10', 'coupled_iteration:9']" / "reader picks for R1: coupled_iteration:9 400.0 kelvin". r1_transfer.py printed: "constructed with arbitrary source_record_id: any-string-at-all 999.0 kelvin".
findings.reproduction: scratchpad/wf/composition-transfer-fields/r10_instants.py and r1_transfer.py (R1d)
findings.fix_direction: Refuse more than one instant per dependency in one run's provenance, or require a declared, ordered instant index. Give QuantityTransfer a check against a ScientificResult (id match plus value lookup, or an explicit 'configured input' source kind) and use it where transfers are built.

verification.reason:
The mechanics are real, but nothing in production reaches the harmful case, so this stays P3 hardening.

What holds up in the code:
- **No check on the fields.** In `QuantityTransfer.__post_init__` (`transfer.py:113-122`), `source_record_id` and `instant` are only checked for being non-empty after strip. Nothing compares them to a result, and the class has no method for that.
- **Instants never collide.** `require_agreeing_transfers` keys on (dependency, instant) and sorts that key as plain strings (`transfer.py:316`). Transfers of one dependency at different instants therefore coexist, and 'coupled_iteration:9' sorts after 'coupled_iteration:10'.
- **Last transfer wins.** `mcp/problem._ambient_by_component` keeps the last transfer for each component.

Why it is not reachable:
- **One instant only.** `ambient_transfers` and `converted_transfers` are the only writers (`coupled.py:2166`). Both take only the final iteration and replace the provenance transfers wholesale, so a production record never holds two instants of one dependency. A real run printed only 'coupled_iteration:4'.
- **Only in-process runs are read.** `_ambient_by_component` only sees the run built in the same process (`problem.py:2189`). No deserialized `CoupledRun` or `ProvenanceRecord` reaches it. The other reader, `evidence.py:1694`, lists every conversion transfer and picks none.
- **The ambient never changes.** The one consumer that picks by last position reads the ambient, which is fixed system configuration: 300 K at iteration 1 and 300 K at iteration 4. A stale ambient transfer could not differ from the final one, so the "stale 400 K beats final 300 K" case needs hand-built records.

Correction to the finding: it says the ambient is "not a value in that result". The named source record does carry the value in `provenance.inputs['ambient_temperature']` (300.0 kelvin, printed below). It is absent only from `result.values`, so the value does trace to that record.

What is left: there is no core API to bind a transfer to its source record, and no ordering rule for instants. A future writer that records several iterations would fall into the ordering trap. That is a hardening gap, P3.

findings.title: Mesh identity depends on floating-point rounding of unit conversion and on a 1e-12 m absolute floor
findings.description: StructuredMesh.fingerprint hashes `repr(length.magnitude_in('meter'))`. Converting 0.7 cm gives 0.006999999999999999 while 7 mm gives 0.007, so one support written in two length units gets two fingerprints. check_field_transfer then answers REQUIRES_PROJECTION with the self-contradictory reason 'one geometry at two resolutions (8x8 against 8x8)'. FieldRecord.verify_against and the conduction2d source check refuse the identical support. This is a false refusal, not false confidence. In the other direction, _same_geometry allows `1e-12 * max(1.0, |left|)` metres, an absolute 1e-12 m floor, so a 10 nm vs 10.0005 nm rectangle counts as the same geometry and gets REQUIRES_PROJECTION where different geometry should be REFUSED. The tolerance is also asymmetric: it scales with the left operand only.
findings.evidence: mesh.py:541-551 (repr of converted floats in the preimage), transfer.py:392-401 and 458-466. r11_fp.py printed: "differing fingerprints for the same length: [(7, '0.007', '0.006999999999999999', '0.007'), (9, ...), (11, ...)]" / "7 mm vs 0.7 cm: requires_projection | one geometry at two resolutions (8x8 against 8x8)". r2_fields.py printed: "10 nm vs 10.0005 nm (0.005% different): requires_projection | one geometry at two resolutions (8x8 against 8x8)".
findings.reproduction: scratchpad/wf/composition-transfer-fields/r11_fp.py and r2_fields.py (R2f)
findings.fix_direction: Canonicalize lengths before hashing, for example by rounding to a declared number of significant digits, or by hashing the authored value and unit plus a tolerance-aware comparison. Make _same_geometry purely relative and symmetric.

verification.reason:
I could not refute this finding. I read the code at 294c129 and ran my own script, and both parts hold. The finding's line numbers are wrong, though. The fingerprint preimage is at mesh.py:210-220, where `_canonical` applies `repr()` to `magnitude_in('meter')`. The tolerance check is at transfer.py:266-275, `1e-12 * max(1.0, abs(left))`, which scales with the left side only. The "two resolutions" branch is at transfer.py:332-340.

Part 1: 0.7 cm converts to 0.006999999999999999 m and 7 mm converts to 0.007 m, so the same support gets two fingerprints. `check_field_transfer` passes `_same_geometry`, then fails the fingerprint test and returns REQUIRES_PROJECTION with the contradictory reason "(8x8 against 8x8)". This affects 265 of the integer millimetre lengths from 1 to 1000 when written in centimetres. The same fingerprint comparison, with no unit normalisation first, is used in `FieldRecord.verify_against` (result.py:160, called by `data/field.py FieldValue.from_record`), in the conduction2d `FieldValue` source check (conduction2d.py:316) and in `FieldObservationOperator.require_support` (field_observation.py:149). All of them would refuse the identical support. I found no other place that normalises units first. A round trip through serialization keeps the declared unit, so that path does not mask the problem or add to it.

Part 2: because the tolerance has an absolute floor of 1e-12 m, 10 nm vs 10.0005 nm and even 1 Å vs 1.009 Å count as the same geometry, and the verdict is REQUIRES_PROJECTION where REFUSED was expected. At 1 mm the floor no longer matters (1 mm vs 1.00001 mm is REFUSED).

Why P3: nothing here grants false confidence. Every wrong verdict is REQUIRES_PROJECTION, so `may_cross_directly` stays False. The unit-spelling case refuses loudly and the user can fix it by declaring both meshes in the same units. The only real harm is losing a valid crossing, plus a misleading reason message. The nanoscale case only matters for rectangles that differ by at most 1e-12 m. The finding is new: the audit document does not mention fingerprint rounding or the geometry tolerance.

findings.title: unresolved_inputs counts any boundary condition, including Neumann/Robin/Periodic/Other, as determining a STATE, so externally_imposed under-reports
findings.description: `determined |= {c.variable for c in problem.boundary_conditions}` ignores BoundaryKind. A STATE pinned only by a flux (Neumann) condition, which fixes no value, or by a PERIODIC or OTHER condition, is reported as resolved. A transient state with a boundary condition but no initial condition also disappears from the set. externally_imposed then returns an empty tuple, and CoupledElectroThermalSystem.unsupplied, which reports rather than refuses, lists nothing for the case of a forgotten supplier.
findings.evidence: dependency.py:522-530. r8_dependency.py printed: "unresolved_inputs: ()" / "externally_imposed (no dependencies): ()" for a STATE with only a NEUMANN condition, against "same state with no condition at all: (('wall2', 'T', 'kelvin'),)".
findings.reproduction: scratchpad/wf/composition-transfer-fields/r8_dependency.py (R8a)
findings.fix_direction: Count only value-fixing kinds (DIRICHLET) as determining a state, or report flux-only states as unresolved with a reason. Consider whether a state needs an initial condition when the problem is transient.

verification.reason: The behaviour is real, but it is not a trust defect, and part of the claim is wrong. In dependency.py:444-445, any BoundaryCondition counts the variable as determined, whatever its kind. I reproduced this for NEUMANN-only, ROBIN-only, PERIODIC-only and OTHER-only STATE variables. Four points count against the finding. (1) Robin: a Robin condition does fix the state's level in a steady problem. The kind-aware check the finding implies would flag it wrongly, which is the same kind of false positive the boundary-condition branch was added to remove. (2) Neumann-only or Periodic-only: the state is under-determined, but that is a well-posedness problem, not a missing input. No other problem supplies "T" into a flux-only problem. The value such a problem actually takes from outside is the flux, and it is already carried on the condition. A Dirichlet condition holding a placeholder value that a composition really supplies reads as resolved too, whatever the kind, so a kind check would not catch the finding's "forgotten supplier" case anyway. (3) The sub-claim about a transient state with no initial condition cannot be represented. ScientificProblem.is_time_dependent is defined as bool(initial_conditions), so the IR itself treats a problem without an initial condition as steady. (4) Reach: unresolved_inputs and externally_imposed only produce a report and never refuse. CoupledElectroThermalSystem.unsupplied has no caller anywhere in src; it is used only in tests. The one real composition (electrothermal lumped) supplies quantities that are CONTROL variables (HEAT_INPUT and AMBIENT_TEMPERATURE, lumped.py:412-425), and the boundary kind never affects CONTROL variables. No scientific conclusion is created, strengthened or kept alive by this. At most it is a P3 hardening note limited to 'a state whose only conditions are NEUMANN or PERIODIC is not flagged as under-determined'. The audit document does not mention it.

findings.title: The energy-crossing fail-closed guard matches only exact energy or power dimensions: flux densities and specific energy cross with no declared conversion
findings.description: QuantityDependency refuses an undeclared conversion only when `dimension in ENERGY_DIMENSIONS`, which is exactly [energy] or [power]. Energy crossing a boundary as a heat flux (W/m2), a line power (W/m), a volumetric source (W/m3) or a specific energy (J/kg) needs no EnergyConversion, and the transfer is recorded as a lossless transport. These are exactly the forms conjugate or field couplings exchange, so writing nothing still means 'all of it arrives' for them. The guard exists to prevent that.
findings.evidence: dependency.py:291-301 and conversion.py:101-104. r8_dependency.py printed: "watt/meter**2 : dependency + transfer ACCEPTED with no EnergyConversion (conversion=None)", the same for watt/meter, joule/kilogram and watt/meter**3, and "watt : REFUSED without conversion ( InvalidScientificProblem )".
findings.reproduction: scratchpad/wf/composition-transfer-fields/r8_dependency.py (R8b)
findings.fix_direction: Treat any dimension that is energy or power divided by length, area, volume, mass or amount as an energy crossing requiring a conversion, or require an explicit 'transport, not conversion' declaration for those dimensions.

verification.reason: The finding holds; I could not refute it. At 294c129, QuantityDependency.__post_init__ (dependency.py:212-222; the finding's line numbers 291-301 are off) only refuses a missing conversion when `self.dimension in ENERGY_DIMENSIONS`. conversion.py:101-104 defines that as exactly two dimensions: energy and power. Any other energy-bearing dimension passes as a plain transport, and the QuantityTransfer is realized with no conversion. That includes heat flux (W/m2), line power (W/m), volumetric source (W/m3), specific energy (J/kg), specific power (W/kg), energy density (J/m3), molar energy (J/mol) and fluence (J/m2). The gap is worse than 'not refused'. A caller cannot declare a loss for these dimensions even if it wants to: EnergyConversion refuses any unit that is not energy or power, a W/m2 dependency is refused if it carries a conversion, and a W/m2 transfer is refused if it carries a source_value. So a lossy flux-density crossing cannot be written down at all. The only accepted form is 'all of it arrives'. The field path (FieldDependency in scientific/fields/transfer.py) has no energy guard at all. Nothing else catches it: the transfer's budget check returns early when there is no conversion. The audit document does not mention it, so it is new. Severity stays P3. No current consumer is affected: the only domain users (systems/electrothermal/coupled.py, resistor_body.py and domains/electrical/dc/models.py) transport power in watts, which the guard does catch. The gap is only reachable through the public API by a future flux or field coupling. It is also partly a design question, because flux continuity at a shared interface is often a real lossless transport. So this is a hardening gap in a fail-closed guard, not unjustified confidence on a current path.

findings.title: Production crossings still carry bare point values: no uncertainty, validity or validation state crosses with a QuantityTransfer
findings.description: This is the stated residual of CORE-016, confirmed from code. QuantityTransfer holds value, source_record_id, instant and source_value, and nothing about the source's uncertainty, validity status or validation outcome. The only uncertainty mechanism (uq/cross_domain) has no src caller. coupled._transport refuses only a source whose validation status is FAIL, so NOT_RUN or WARNING sources, and sources outside their validated domain, cross unmarked. dc_models._received_ambient turns the transfer into a point Quantity that feeds `declared` for the resistor derating verdict. It checks target_quantity but not that target_problem_id is this resistor's problem, and it uses setdefault, so an ambient the problem already declares silently overrides the transfer. The consuming verdict therefore cannot reflect a weak or unknown upstream result. Electrothermal results currently state UNKNOWN uncertainty throughout, so the practical effect today is on validity and credibility, not on numbers.

The audit doc's CORE-016 residual: 'QuantityTransfer carries no upstream credibility, and nothing combines uncertainty sources'.
findings.fix_direction: Give QuantityTransfer an optional, bound upstream-evidence field: the source result's uncertainty entry for source_quantity, its validation status and its validity status. Route electrothermal transfers through make_uncertainty_transfer. In domain consumers, check the target problem id and refuse a conflicting declared value instead of using setdefault.

verification.reason:
The main claim holds, and the audit doc already lists it as the CORE-016 residual ("QuantityTransfer carries no upstream credibility"). Two of the finding's sub-claims are overstated or wrong, and its practical effect is smaller than described.

Confirmed from the code:
- **Fields:** `QuantityTransfer` has only dependency, value, source_record_id, instant and source_value (checked at runtime).
- **Unused uncertainty path:** `propagate_transfer_uncertainty`, `make_uncertainty_transfer`, `propagate_uncertainty_chain` and `UncertaintyTransfer` appear in src only inside `uq/cross_domain.py`. Their only other user is `tests/test_cross_domain_uq.py`. So the doc's "cross-domain transfer carries it" describes code no production crossing uses.
- **Transport bar:** `coupled.transportable` is `status is not FAIL` (coupled.py:738). WARNING and NOT_RUN sources, and the source's validity status, cross unmarked. The docstring says this is deliberate.
- **No target check:** `_received_ambient` compares only target_quantity. The repro shows a transfer declared for R999 accepted on R1's problem and driving the verdict (OUTSIDE_VALIDATED_DOMAIN). In production this cannot happen: `_ambient_by_component` sends each transfer to the resistor named by its target_problem_id.

Refuted or overstated:
- **setdefault:** The claim that a problem-declared ambient "silently overrides the transfer" is wrong for the verdict. `assess_resistor_validity` passes the transfer's value to `resistor_rating_context`, and the derating verdict is computed from that. With the problem declaring 400 K and the transfer 300 K, the result is satisfied. With 300 K declared and 400 K transferred, it is violated. The problem's value survives only in the declared-half map, which no resistor condition reads (`evaluated` is empty). Production `resistor_relation_problem` declares only `resistance`, so even that divergence cannot arise there.
- **Weak upstream result:** The ambient that crosses is `stage.body.ambient_temperature`, the thermal body's own declared input, not something the thermal solve computed. That solve's validation or validity cannot make the ambient less trustworthy.
- **Report level:** `run_electrothermal_case` builds its report over the dependency closure and gives a verdict for every model in it. System-level credibility does not depend on the transfer record carrying that state.

This is a real, already-documented design gap with no demonstrated case of unjustified confidence on a normal path, so it stays at P3 (residual).

findings.title: CORE-014 binding is bypassed on the report path both MCP tools use, and does nothing for derived condition values even when a caller opts in
findings.description:
The CORE-014 fix compares an assessment's recorded `evaluated` values with `provenance.inputs` in one place only: `ScientificResult.__post_init__`. Both MCP tools build their validity verdicts somewhere else. The boundary calls the domain `assess_*` functions and hands the records to `CredibilityEvidenceReport.from_result(validity=...)`, and `_merged_validity` / `ModelValidityRecord` never read `evaluated`. So an assessment made at another operating point, even one built with `record_values=True`, becomes a SUPPORTED credibility verdict. That verdict also survives `to_dict`/`from_dict`.

The guard is also empty on every production path, for two reasons:
1. Nothing in src passes `record_values=True`. No domain assessment function, context `.assess`, MCP assembler or study does.
2. When a caller does opt in, a recorded name is compared only if that name is also a provenance input. Across the 16 registered models, 59 of the 77 names that validity conditions read are reserved derived quantities, such as `linear_resistance_ratio`, Biot or utilization ratios. Those are recorded but never compared, and neither are the inputs behind them (for example `temperature_coefficient`), because those are not condition keys.

findings.title: The only production calibration study predicts and validates through frozen V1 functions, so the goodness-of-fit, containment, prior and prediction-domain guards never run
findings.description:
`engcore.hybrid_uq` has no caller in src outside its own package; `api_snapshot.py` only lists it. It is reached only from tests and `benchmarks/core_v2_hybrid_uq/audit`.

The production orchestration layer that turns a calibration into predictive intervals and a held-out verdict (`studies/calibration_study.py`: `predict_held_out`, `validate_held_out`, `run_coverage_study`) uses V1 `gaussian_grid_posterior` + `uq.predictive.posterior_predictive_uq`. `adequacy.assess_predictive_observation` uses the same V1 path. That path checks none of the following:
- whether the declared noise explains the calibration residuals (CORE-001);
- whether the grid box contains the posterior (CORE-002);
- whether node spacing is the declared prior (CORE-010);
- whether the prediction lies inside the calibrated conditions (CORE-006).

`posterior_predictive_uq` silently ignores `PredictiveObservableSpec.conditions`, and its result has no claim or reason field to carry a downgrade. The result:
- A truncated grid yields parameter sd 2.8x too small, with no refusal or flag, and held-out validation still PASSes.
- A calibration whose residuals are 10x the declared sigma still gets predictive intervals from `predict_held_out`.
- A spec declaring T = 5000 K is predicted without comment.

The audit's residuals state that V1 `posterior_predictive_uq` and `gaussian_grid_posterior` are unchanged for CORE-001 and CORE-010. They do not state that the one production study runs on them, nor that containment (CORE-002) and prediction conditions (CORE-006) are absent there.

findings.title: The MCP verdict an agent reads never carries evidence_basis, although every SUPPORTED MCP verdict is verification-only by construction
findings.description:
The CORE-008 fix left the verdict word unchanged and added `verdict_qualifiers.evidence_basis` inside the serialized credibility report. The MCP transport builds the agent-facing verdict (`_verdict_block`: value, means, does_not_mean, action, verdict_reasons, other_findings) and the `describe_capabilities` verdict guidance from `_VERDICT_GUIDANCE` and `_fired_rules`. Neither mentions evidence basis. The SUPPORTED `means` text reads: "at least one check both passed and established an evidentiary level".

In both MCP tools no validation level is reachable at all:
- `_TRUSTED_ORACLE_DECLARATIONS` is empty, so BENCHMARK_VALIDATED and EXPERIMENTALLY_VALIDATED cannot be issued.
- The only cross-solver check is deliberately stripped of its level (`_withhold_level`).

Every SUPPORTED verdict an agent can receive is therefore VERIFICATION_ONLY. The published example case in `describe_capabilities`, which the tool description says 'can be SUPPORTED', is one of them. The qualifier exists only two levels down, in `stages[i].report.verdict_qualifiers`.

src/engcore/mcp/evidence.py:1770-1771: the only place evidence_basis is emitted.
src/engcore/mcp/problem.py:1437-1454 (_withhold_level).
src/engcore/scientific/oracles.py:85-87: empty registry.

mcp_core008.py output:
  verdict block: supported | verdict_reasons: [] | other_findings: []
  means: Nothing in this report argues against relying on the result, and at least one check both passed and established an evidentiary level.
  'evidence_basis' or 'verification' in verdict block: False False
  report.verdict_qualifiers.evidence_basis: VERIFICATION_ONLY
  'evidence_basis' anywhere in describe_capabilities: False | 'VERIFICATION_ONLY': False
  pinned oracles (only issuers of BENCHMARK/EXPERIMENTALLY_VALIDATED): {}
findings.reproduction: Run <scratch>/reach-and-adoption/mcp_core008.py. It calls `server.run_electrothermal(example_electrothermal_payload())` and inspects `stages[0].verdict` against `stages[0].report.verdict_qualifiers`.
findings.fix_direction: Carry `evidence_basis` in `_verdict_block`, next to value, means and does_not_mean. Add a non-deciding fired rule (like `check_warned`) such as `verification_only`, naming the attained verification levels. State in `_VERDICT_GUIDANCE`/`describe_capabilities` that SUPPORTED with VERIFICATION_ONLY says the model was solved correctly, not that it describes the part.

verification.reason:
I could not refute the behaviour; it happens as described.
- `_verdict_block` (server.py:338-363) only emits value, means, does_not_mean, action, verdict_reasons and other_findings.
- `_fired_rules` has no evidence-basis rule.
- Neither `describe_capabilities` nor `_VERDICT_GUIDANCE` mentions evidence_basis, verification or validation.
- The published electrothermal example returns SUPPORTED, while the same response's report says `evidence_basis` is VERIFICATION_ONLY.

The claim that no MCP run can reach VALIDATED also holds:
- `_TRUSTED_ORACLE_DECLARATIONS` is an empty MappingProxyType, and no MCP payload route supplies oracle evidence.
- The only cross-solver check goes through `_withhold_level` (establishes=None).
- The checks on the electrothermal and battery paths establish only DIMENSIONALLY_VALID, NUMERICALLY_CONVERGED or ANALYTICALLY_VERIFIED.
So every SUPPORTED an agent can get over MCP is verification-only by construction.

I lowered the severity from P2 to P3 for three reasons:
1. Nothing is lost or weakened. The same tool response carries the qualifier and the attained levels in `stages[i].report.verdict_qualifiers` (and in `report.verdict_qualifiers` for battery). The CORE-008 fix is re-derived on read and reaches the agent.
2. The SUPPORTED guidance already warns the reader. `does_not_mean` says it "does not mean the result is right, that the model is accurate", and it tells the reader to "Read the checks, the levels they established".
3. The main point is already a stated residual. The audit doc's CORE-008 row says "SUPPORTED on verification alone is still SUPPORTED, now visibly qualified" and leaves the verdict word to the owner.

What is new is narrower: the verdict summary and the capability prose an agent reads first were never updated to surface the qualifier. That is a communication-hardening gap in the transport layer, not a guard bypass in the generic core.

findings.title: evidence_basis labels agreement between two solvers of the same declared model as VALIDATED
findings.description:
`VALIDATION_LEVELS` puts CROSS_SOLVER_VALIDATED beside BENCHMARK_VALIDATED and EXPERIMENTALLY_VALIDATED as a level that 'compare[s] a result with something outside the model that produced it'. `evidence_basis` returns VALIDATED whenever any of them is attained.

The pinned cross-solver routes compare two implementations of one declared problem:
- DC native MNA versus ngspice both declare `problem_declaration: py:engcore.domains.electrical.dc.circuit:DCCircuit`, and the consensus itself lists that as a shared dependency.
- The CSTR BDF and Radau routes both declare `ReactorRun`.

Agreement there is code-to-code verification of the declared model. It says nothing about whether the circuit model describes the hardware. Yet a DC result whose only other levels are dimensional validity and convergence moves from VERIFICATION_ONLY to VALIDATED once the consensus check is attached. That repeats, inside the qualifier, the solution-versus-world confusion CORE-008 was fixed to expose.

Reach: the `dc_consensus` API and `execution.consensus` trusted decisions can attach this level. The MCP boundary withholds it, and the CSTR cross-method arm awards none.

src/engcore/domains/__init__.py:179-213: both DC routes share problem_declaration DCCircuit.

  native levels: ['dimensionally_valid', 'numerically_converged'] basis: VERIFICATION_ONLY
  with the consensus check -> evidence_basis: VALIDATED | levels: ['cross_solver_validated', 'dimensionally_valid', 'numerically_converged']

2. Compute `dc_consensus(...).to_check()` and add it with `native.validation.with_check(check)`.
3. Read `.evidence_basis`.
findings.fix_direction: Classify CROSS_SOLVER_VALIDATED as verification unless the routes are independent in problem declaration, i.e. different models of the same system. Alternatively, make `evidence_basis` three-valued (EXTERNAL_DATA / CODE_TO_CODE / VERIFICATION_ONLY). Restrict VALIDATED to comparisons with data from outside any declared model, such as EXPERIMENTAL, or BENCHMARK when the oracle is measured data.

verification.reason:
I could not refute it; it reproduces. Checked in D:/forge-audit at 294c129.

1. `VALIDATION_LEVELS` (validation.py:393-397) puts CROSS_SOLVER_VALIDATED beside BENCHMARK and EXPERIMENTAL validation.
2. `evidence_basis` (validation.py:803-816) returns VALIDATED when any of those three levels is attained.
3. The consensus core (scientific/consensus.py) guarantees the routes share the problem being solved. `SOLVER_INDEPENDENCE_DIMENSIONS` leaves out the problem declaration, and the core's own docstring says a declaration error "is invisible to every route that reads it".
4. The pinned DC routes (domains/__init__.py:179-213) both declare DCCircuit. The live consensus shows that shared declaration, rates the routes PARTIALLY_INDEPENDENT with `routes_are_independent` True, and awards the level.

So agreement between two solvers of one model moves the label from VERIFICATION_ONLY to VALIDATED. That contradicts the code's own definition of these levels: "compare a result with something outside the model that produced it". An adversarial case confirms it: a circuit declared with a wrong resistor value (R2 = 30 kohm) is still labelled VALIDATED, because both solvers agree about the wrong model.

Reach:
- The label appears on the Python API: `result.validation.with_check(dc_consensus(...).to_check())`. It also appears in a directly built `CredibilityEvidenceReport`, whose `verdict_qualifiers.evidence_basis` reads VALIDATED.
- `TrustedConsensusGate` in execution/consensus.py can award the same level.
- The electrothermal MCP path does not reach it: `_withhold_level` in mcp/problem.py:1434-1455 removes the level. Battery MCP attaches no cross-solver check, and nothing else serializes `evidence_basis`.
- The label is a qualifier only; the verdict word does not change.

I kept P2 rather than raising it: this is a generic core rule that quietly defeats the CORE-008 qualifier for every cross-solver result, but the one normal serialized path is shielded. I lowered no further because the rule is generic, not domain-specific.

New versus residual: the audit document lists only one residual for CORE-008 (the verdict word is unchanged). It says nothing about cross-solver agreement counting as validation, so this is new and was introduced by the CORE-008 fix.

findings.title: CORE-015's established-candidate rule is absent from the selection path production actually uses: design Pareto and elite archives rank unassessed candidates
findings.description:
CORE-015 made `ScientificExperiment.best` rank only evaluations whose results name models that were all assessed IN_DOMAIN. Nothing in src calls `.best(` or constructs a `ScientificExperiment`.

The selection mechanism production does use is `design.ParetoArchive` / `ScopedEliteArchive`, through the multirotor MVR0/MVR1 studies. Its eligibility gate is a caller-set `SelectionEligibility.ELIGIBLE` with a free-text reason and never consults `result.validity`. The multirotor studies mark every evaluation ELIGIBLE, although every result carries `validity_not_assessed` for both models. The result is a global Pareto front, plus a per-objective 'elite' (the single best by mass, endurance or hover power), chosen entirely from candidates for which `_established()` is False.

The audit residual says an unassessed evaluation 'is recorded, not ranked'. On this path it is ranked.

findings.fix_direction: Share one established-candidate rule: extract `_established` into the results layer and apply it in `ParetoArchive.build` / `ScopedEliteArchive.build` or in `DesignEvaluation`. ELIGIBLE should require all result models to be IN_DOMAIN. Otherwise the archive should be labelled as ranking unassessed candidates, e.g. a SelectionEligibility value distinct from ELIGIBLE.

verification.reason:
I could not refute the mechanics; they reproduce at 294c129. `_established()` and the CORE-015 filter exist only in `ScientificExperiment.best` (experiment.py:63-72, 183-208), and nothing under src calls it. `design/archives.py` admits a candidate only on the caller-set `SelectionEligibility.ELIGIBLE` (`_require_eligible`, `_pareto_refs`) and never reads `result.validity`. The same is true of `ScopedEliteArchive.build` and `validate_against`. MVR1 hard-codes ELIGIBLE (study.py:742), and `MultirotorStudyRun.__post_init__` refuses anything else. Every result carries `validity_not_assessed` for both models. So a Pareto front and three per-objective elites are picked from 24 candidates, and none of the 24 is established. The endurance elite also fails the study's own targets. Nothing else refuses this, and the audit doc covers CORE-015 only for Experiment.best, so this is a new finding, not a residual.

I lower the severity from P2 to P3 for four reasons:
(1) Calling this "the selection path production actually uses" overstates its reach. The only callers are a reference-benchmark CLI (experiments/multirotor_mvr1/run.py) and tests. MCP does not reach design archives, and nothing in src consumes D3 memory.
(2) The records themselves carry disclaimers: the eligibility reason says eligibility "does not imply target satisfaction or physical feasibility", and each result carries a "not physical validation" warning and `validity_not_assessed` per model.
(3) No model in the study declares a validity domain, so ranking does not push out any established candidate.
(4) Archive membership is a non-dominance fact about computed values, not a conclusion the core states as established.

What remains is an adoption gap. The generic design selection layer has no hook that is aware of validity, and the CLI summary prints Pareto member ids without the validity or warning context.

findings.title: CORE-006 reads the calibrated range from whatever observation set the caller passes; nothing ties it to the posterior
findings.description:
The following take `calibration_observations` as a free argument:
- `linearized_predictive_uq(..., calibration_observations=)`
- `routed_predictive_uncertainty(..., calibration_observations=)`

`_prediction_domain_reasons` computes the calibrated per-condition range from that set, and nothing checks the set against the posterior. A `LocalGaussianPosterior` records `dataset_id`, and it is never compared, so not even the label binding CORE-007 was criticised for exists here.

Passing any observation set whose declared conditions span the prediction point turns a DOWNGRADED `PREDICTION_OUTSIDE_CALIBRATED_CONDITIONS` extrapolation into a SUPPORTED prediction with no reasons. The grid path in `grid_predictive_uncertainty` is bound by content, because the same `observations` are re-evaluated against the grid. The linearized path and the `routed_predictive_uncertainty` grid path are not.
findings.evidence:
src/engcore/hybrid_uq/predictive.py:285-302 (_prediction_domain_reasons: no posterior argument), :311-318, :414.
src/engcore/hybrid_uq/router.py:676-702: calibration_observations is passed through unchecked.
src/engcore/hybrid_uq/local_gaussian.py:691 and :1207: the posterior does carry dataset_id.

  posterior dataset_id: synthetic.CORE006 claim: SUPPORTED
  with the posterior's own observations: DOWNGRADED ['PREDICTION_OUTSIDE_CALIBRATED_CONDITIONS']
  with an unrelated 2-point set (dataset 'some.other.dataset') spanning x in [0, 1e5]: SUPPORTED [] | total interval (19517.64, 21320.46)
findings.reproduction:
Run <scratch>/reach-and-adoption/core006_unbound_domain.py:
1. Build the affine synthetic problem (tests/hybrid_uq/hybrid_synthetic.py, `S.conditioned`) and `local_gaussian_posterior` with MultistartPolicy.
2. Predict at x=1e4 with `calibration_observations` = the posterior's own set, which gives DOWNGRADED.
3. Predict again with a fabricated ObservationSet under another dataset_id, conditions x=0 and x=1e5, which gives SUPPORTED.
findings.fix_direction: Bind the calibration observations to the posterior by content: require `calibration_observations.dataset_id == posterior.dataset_id`, and check an observation-content digest recorded on the posterior (its sensitivity digest already covers the residual vector). For a `HybridUQResult`, record the calibration set's digest at routing time and refuse any other set.

verification.reason:
The finding holds, and the gap is wider than it says.

What the code does:
- `_prediction_domain_reasons(spec, calibration_observations)` (predictive.py:285-308) builds the calibrated range only from whatever set the caller passes.
- `linearized_predictive_uq` (:318, :414) and `routed_predictive_uncertainty` (router.py:686, :700, :712) never compare that set with the posterior. There is no dataset_id check, and no check of keys or values against the sensitivity record. This is so even though `LocalGaussianPosterior` carries `dataset_id` (local_gaussian.py:691, :1207), and the router already compares dataset_id for supplied grids (router.py:528).

What I reproduced:
- **Linearized route:** the honest call gives DOWNGRADED `PREDICTION_OUTSIDE_CALIBRATED_CONDITIONS`. With an unrelated set under another dataset_id, it gives SUPPORTED with no reasons.
- **A realistic mistake:** passing the calibration set plus one held-out point at x=2e4 also turns the x=1e4 extrapolation SUPPORTED.
- **`routed_predictive_uncertainty`, GRID_AS_SUPPLIED result:** the honest set gives DOWNGRADED, the unrelated set gives SUPPORTED.
- **Routed LOCAL_GAUSSIAN result:** the extrapolation reason disappears. The claim stays DOWNGRADED here only because GLOBAL_UNIQUENESS_NOT_ASSESSED is also present.

Correction to the finding: it says the standalone `grid_predictive_uncertainty` path is "bound by content". That is only partly true. The grid-evidence check binds the observation values and sigmas, not the declared conditions. A set with identical values but every condition scaled by 1e5 (same dataset_id) passes and gives SUPPORTED. So the calibrated range can be widened on all three entry points.

Why P2 and not P1: the caller has to pass a set other than the one the posterior was calibrated on, so this is misuse or a mistake, not the default path. Also, `spec.conditions` is itself never checked against what `predict` actually evaluates, so the guard rests on the caller's declarations throughout. Still, a wrong set silently turns an extrapolation from DOWNGRADED into SUPPORTED, and the cheap bindings are missing. That fits P2.

Residual or new: new. The audit's CORE-006 residual lists three things: the per-condition box, the predictor not being bound to the calibrated model, and domains not declaring conditions. It does not mention that calibration_observations are unbound.

findings.title: CORE-016 source_kind has no producer, and the one consumer that combines uncertainty channels (SRIA budget) never reads it
findings.description:
No code in src sets `Uncertainty.source_kind`. Every domain solver emits `Uncertainty.unknown`. V1 `posterior_predictive_uq` builds its epistemic interval (known to be PARAMETER) and its total interval (known to be COMBINED) as UNSPECIFIED. `propagate_transfer_uncertainty` copies the field but has no caller.

The audit residual says 'nothing combines uncertainty sources', but SRIA's `UncertaintyBudget` does. Its `ChannelEntry` files an `Uncertainty` under an ALEATORIC / EPISTEMIC_PARAMETER / MODEL_FORM / NUMERICAL channel, `aggregate` root-sum-squares channels, and `NumericalCritic` passes `numerical_uncertainty_declared` from the NUMERICAL channel. None of this reads `source_kind`, so the record the fix added to stop a discretization estimate standing in for scientific uncertainty is never compared with the channel it is filed under. A record saying NUMERICAL is accepted and aggregated as aleatoric plus parameter uncertainty, and a MEASUREMENT record passes as the numerical channel.

findings.title: CORE-013 precedence makes older stored results unreadable and makes SRIA report 'validation was never run' when a check simply did not apply
findings.description:
`ValidationReport.from_dict` refuses any payload whose serialized `status` differs from the recomputed one. The pre-branch rule (FAIL > WARNING > PASS > NOT_RUN) wrote 'pass' for a report with passing checks plus a NOT_RUN. Domains emit exactly that shape for checks that do not apply, e.g. the DC solver's `voltage_source_relation` NOT_RUN when a circuit has no voltage source. Every `ScientificResult` stored that way before this branch (via `ScientificResult.from_dict`, `CoupledRun.from_dict`, `DesignEvaluation.from_dict`) is now refused on read.

Separately, SRIA's `NumericalCritic` maps `status is NOT_RUN` to NOT_ASSESSED with the fixed detail 'validation was never run'. That detail is now false for a report in which five checks ran and passed and one was inapplicable.

Both effects are conservative (they lose or under-state evidence rather than overstate it). The audit residual notes the NOT_RUN ambiguity but not these consumers.

The `validation_report` schema string was not bumped. `ValidationReport.from_dict` (validation.py:902-906) still refuses any payload whose written status differs from the recomputed one.
   - I did not hand-edit a payload to test this. I used `git archive` (read-only) to export the real pre-branch tree from base commit 9361b97, the merge of PR #47. findings.title: The decisive model comparison (CORE-007/011) has no production caller, and its content-binding gate trusts a constructor flag
findings.description:
`compare_log_predictive_scores` is never called in src.

The TCR study builds content-bound assessments in `validate_held_out`, then reduces them to residuals and log densities and discards them, so no production path can feed a comparison.

The comparison names a preferred model when every assessment has `content_bound=True`. `content_bound` is a plain dataclass field that any caller can pass to the `PredictiveObservationAssessment` constructor, not only a read-back value. `__post_init__` never checks it. Hand-built assessments therefore get a decisive 'preferred_model'.

The binding also covers only the posterior and the observed value. It does not cover the predictive table or the `model` label the preference is issued for.

The audit residual covers only the read-back case ('A read-back content_bound is integrity-only').

I tried to refute each part of the finding and could not. All of it holds, and P3 is the right severity.

1. **No production caller.** In src, `compare_log_predictive_scores` shows up only where it is defined (adequacy/predictive.py:538) and in the re-export in adequacy/__init__.py. The only real call sites are in tests and in experiments/kinetics_k4/k4_run.py. That script does not pass `split` or `calibration_table`, and it reads `delta_a_minus_b > 0` itself rather than `preferred_model`.

2. **The study throws its assessments away.** In calibration_study.py:400-420, `validate_held_out` builds content-bound assessments but keeps only their residuals, log densities, errors and coverage. `HeldOutMetrics` has no field for the assessments. So the audit's residual line "the TCR study passes both" is true, but nothing in src ever feeds a comparison.

3. **`content_bound` is a plain field anyone can set.** It is declared at predictive.py:210, and `__post_init__` (212-256) never checks it. The gate at 606 only reads it. As a result, `dataclasses.replace(unbound, content_bound=True)` turns a refused comparison into a decisive `preferred_model`. The original script reproduces the same thing with hand-built records.

4. **The binding covers only the posterior and the observed value.** `_require_posterior_conditioned_on_calibration` (inference/split.py:373) checks the posterior against the calibration table and the calibration half. `posterior_predictive_uq` checks that the predictive table's points match the posterior's points, but not its values. `AdmittedForwardTable` carries no model identity. So a content-bound record can use another model's predictive table, or carry the wrong model label, and the comparison accepts it.

**Residual or new.** The audit doc (line 125) states only that "A read-back `content_bound` is integrity-only", which covers the `from_dict` path. Building the record directly or through `dataclasses.replace`, and the gaps in item 4, are not stated there, so they are new. They are the same kind of problem as that residual, though. Anyone who builds a record by hand can also invent `log_predictive_density`, so the flag gives no extra power to fake a result. With no src caller, no normal path reaches this. The one overstatement is the audit calling CORE-007 "FIXED (… comparisons require it)", when that requirement is a flag the caller sets. This is hardening and an adoption gap, not a way to get unjustified confidence on a normal path.

All three behaviours happen, but the finding makes them sound worse than they are. The real issue is a migration and hardening gap, not a P2 trust gap.

(1) validation_report/1 (validation.py:902-906): the new reader refuses a report written by base 9361b97 whose checks are PASS plus NOT_RUN. The old reader also refuses a report the branch writes over the same checks. Both refusals are loud and correct. The stored 'pass' is exactly the overclaim CORE-013 removed, so this is not a justified verdict being refused. Dropping the status key makes the report load and recompute to not_run. The V1 fixture for this record is an empty ValidationReport() (benchmarks/core_freeze_v1/audit/reproduce.py:125), so it is true that no freeze inventory sees this change in meaning.

(2) Hybrid records: the claim that "no freeze inventory can see" this is false here. On the audit head, the V3 verifier's serialization_facts() raises HybridUQError while building its own fixtures. The audit document says the V1/V2/V3 manifest tests fail by design until Core Freeze V4, and that route_diagnostics/1 records are refused. The refused RoutedIdentifiability also stores condition_number 4.0, computed on the covariance under the definition CORE-004 retired, while the correlation value is 1.0. The reader cannot tell which definition a stored number used, so refusing it protects the reader. It is not a justified verdict lost for one sentence. HybridUQResult and LocalGaussianPosterior are refused, with reasons, through their embedded /1 diagnostics.

(3) Reverse direction: reproduced. An older reader silently drops 'evaluated' and 'source_kind'. After one re-emit, the branch accepts a result at T=5000 K as IN_DOMAIN from an assessment that was bound to 300 K. Four things limit this. It needs an opt-in writer, and no production caller uses record_values=True or sets source_kind (only a test does). It needs an older-version consumer in the loop. The stripped record is identical to a default one, and the audit's CORE-014/CORE-016 residuals already state that an assessment without record_values binds nothing and that UNSPECIFIED is the default. Removing the key by hand is equally possible, and the core disclaims digests as authority. Nothing gates on source_kind. What is left is a schema-versioning and migration note for the V4 round: P3, not a normal-path confidence gap.

The behaviour is real, but I'd rate it P3, not P2.

What the code does:
- V3's assurance check (tools/certification/core_freeze_v3.py lines 318-337) looks only at the assurance JSON: schema, manifest sha, candidate, `green` flags, formal killed/population and population_sha256, and trust `killed == population > 0`. The population sha is public and recomputed from the tree.
- It never opens the `evidence` files, never checks their digests or the recorded measurement commits, and never uses `mutation_population.log_problems` or `coverage_problems`, even though both exist.
- V2's check (core_freeze_v2.py lines 331-349) is the same kind: `killed==79`, `hd_matrix` and wheel "MATCH" are all taken from the JSON.
- V1's `verify_assurance` (core_freeze.py lines 700-801) does re-derive: evidence hashes, the 79-log tally, and `suites.commit == candidate`.
- Nothing else stops a false record. The V3 manifest tests only call `verify()`, and no CI workflow runs the V3 verifier. The builder (benchmarks/core_freeze_v3/audit/build_assurance.py `freeze()`) checks shard-log digests when it writes the record, but it never compares the suites, formal or trust commits with the candidate. So a record measured at the wrong commit would get past both the builder and the verifier.

What I ran (only the V1 verify, certificate facts and serialization facts were stubbed; the assurance JSON sat in scratch):
- A made-up record with no evidence, bare `{green: true}` suites and a trust population of 1/1 passes all six assurance checks.
- The committed record with every evidence digest set to zero, commits set to deadbeef, suite exit codes 1 and trust survived=7 also passes all six.

Why P3 rather than P2:
- (a) This is certification tooling, not the scientific core, and no scientific result changes.
- (b) Getting past it takes a committed record that is wrong or measured at the wrong commit, which a reviewer would see in git.
- (c) The real V3 record is consistent. All 7 evidence digests match. Suites were measured at 656dea7, which has no src/tests/tools diff from candidate 9acffc0. Trust was measured at 999dbdf, an ancestor with no src diff but 21 fewer lines of test code (killing a mutant can only get easier with more tests). Formal shards 0 and 3 were run at b8b13b2 and shards 1 and 2 at 2ade43d. The two mutation definitions that changed (G29aj, G29ao) sit in shards 1 and 2, which were the ones re-run.
- (d) On this branch the V3 verifier cannot pass anyway. Unstubbed, `serialization_facts()` raises HybridUQError (the V3 fixture records are now refused). With it stubbed, `v1.symbols_preserved`, `api.unchanged_from_v2` and `v3.vocabulary` fail. The audit doc says the V1/V2/V3 verifiers fail here by design.
- (e) The harm to a V4 freeze is only a possibility for now.

Also, `test_mutation_harness.py` checks that every mutation still applies, so the stale patterns would be refused once they are folded in.
- **"No attribution" is overstated.** Each batch run executes one named test and logs pytest's last summary line ("1 failed").
- **The headline gap is residual, not new.** The audit doc says nothing is certified yet, that the core certificate and Core Freeze V1/V2/V3 checks fail on this branch by design, and that the batch mutations join tests/mutation_guards.py in the Core Freeze V4 round. verification.reason:
The mechanism is real, but it does less damage than the finding claims, so I rate it P3, not P2.

What I confirmed in the code:
- The `harness` area in `tools/certification/core_certificate.py` (lines 329-389) lists exactly `tests/mutation_guards.py` plus the 48 `TARGETS` files, and `enumerate_area` hashes only files that match those patterns.
- The helper modules those suites import are not in any area, and my own AST import scan reproduces the reported counts. `hybrid_synthetic.py` is used by 10 targets, `route_declarations_for_tests.py` by 5, `test_sria_m3_assurance.py` by 5 and `sria_m5_benchmark.py` by 3.
- The stored certificate (certified commit 4033c22, an ancestor of HEAD) has no entry for `hybrid_synthetic.py`. `verify_certificate` lists 7 modified harness files and not the helper, even though the helper changed since that commit.
- Nothing checks that `TARGETS` and the harness patterns agree. They match today only because someone kept them in step by hand.
- The same gap exists in a second place, which the finding did not mention. The cross-commit shard check in `benchmarks/core_freeze_v3/audit/build_assurance.py` (~line 108) runs `git diff` over only `src` and `TARGETS`. The shards can therefore pass that check while seeing different helper bytes, even though its own comment says nothing a mutation or its suites read may have moved.
- The docs/audits/CORE_SCIENTIFIC_AUDIT_2026-09-16.md audit document does not mention this gap, so "new" is the right label.

Why I refute part of it and lower the severity:
1. **Recertification still triggers.** `recertification_scope.ADDITIONAL_TRIGGERS` has an `assurance_suites` entry for `tests/**`, and asking it about the helper path returns `['assurance_suites']`. `OUT_OF_SCOPE` also says openly that `tests/**` outside the harness is not certified. So no gate is bypassed. What weakens is only what a byte-verified certificate means, and only for someone who checks a later commit with the default CLI (`--require-commit` off) after the CI trigger was skipped.
2. **The branch's change did nothing harmful.** The diff since 9361b97, and since the certified commit, only adds a new function, `conditioned()`. No existing Problem object, observation or scenario byte changed, so no kill was weakened. The `observed=` change the finding mentions is not in that diff.
3. **The certificate already fails on this branch.** Verification reports drift in the core, evidence_identity, harness, inference_admission, predictive_representation and routed_uncertainty areas, so the helper change could not hide behind a passing certificate.
4. **This is not a scientific-conclusion path.** It concerns what the certificate means, not whether the core states a result too confidently. The harness area also cannot be a full transitive closure by design: `src/engcore/domains/**` and `conftest.py` are unpinned as well.

It is a real gap between what the harness area says it pins and what it pins, with no binding check. It can matter only if the CI trigger is bypassed, which makes it hardening (P3).

The facts hold, but I'd call it P3, not P2.

What the code shows: `describe()` in `api_snapshot.py` (lines 283-338) records only the constructor signature, dataclass fields, enum members, exception MRO and constant values, and `build()` only describes names listed in `__all__`. I confirmed each part of the claim with a run:
- The entries for ValidityDomain, ValidationReport, ScientificExperiment and ScientificResult hold no methods or properties.
- I stripped `record_values` from `ValidityDomain.assess`, deleted `ValidationReport.evidence_basis` and `ScientificExperiment.best`, and wrapped `OracleEvidenceSet.compare` so it no longer declares `conditions`. Neither the V1 nor the V2 frozen digest moved.
- UncertaintySource is not exported from `engcore.scientific` or `engcore.scientific.results`, and OracleEvidenceSet is in no canonical `__all__`. The V2 frozen bytes never contain 'model_form', 'numerical', 'VERIFICATION_ONLY', 'record_values' or 'evidence_basis'.
- Field additions from the fixes are caught: diffing the live snapshot against `tests/api/frozen_api_snapshot.json` shows `Uncertainty.source_kind`, `ValidityAssessment.evaluated`, `PredictiveObservationAssessment.content_bound`, the `conditions` fields and the new `ModelScoreComparison` fields.

So the claim that a V4 built with this tool would freeze the field shapes but not the calls is correct. The audit doc does not mention it. It only says the V1/V2 snapshots fail by design until V4, and the owner's V4 rule says nothing may be removed or changed, which this tool cannot enforce for methods. So this counts as new.

Why P3 and not P2:
1. The blind spot is not specific to the fixes. It has been there since V1 and covers every method in the frozen API.
2. The snapshot is an API-compatibility guard, not a check on scientific confidence. Nothing here produces or strengthens a conclusion on any current path. It only matters if a later code change goes in.
3. Removing any of the named items would fail loudly at call sites, not silently. `record_values=` would raise TypeError. `evidence_basis` is read in `mcp/evidence.py` line 1771, so removing it raises AttributeError.
4. A silent weakening, such as looser `best()` eligibility or a different evidence_basis rule, would not show up in a snapshot of method signatures either, so recording methods would not close that risk.
5. The unexported UncertaintySource is only a minor adoption gap: `Uncertainty(source_kind="numerical")` is converted to the enum member. What is really left open is that its member vocabulary and the evidence_basis strings are not frozen.

findings.title: No additive-only comparator: a V4 --build certifies whatever the live API is, and 'v1_entries_byte_identical_in_v2' is a live-versus-live tautology
findings.description: The owner's V4 rule (recorded in the audit document) is 'may add to V1-frozen symbols and may not remove or change anything'. No tool implements it: V1 compares digests for equality, and V2/V3 build_manifest store live api_facts(). Inside api_facts, v1_entries_byte_identical_in_v2 compares entries of api_snapshot.build() with entries of api_snapshot.build(modules=V2_CANONICAL_MODULES), both from the live tree, so it is True whatever changed; on this branch it is True while 7 V1 entries changed, and a V4 manifest copying the V2/V3 builder would record 'true' as a certification fact. (tests/test_core_v2_compatibility.py does compare against the pinned file, but it asserts equality, so it cannot express 'additive'.) findings.title: Analytic admission route is a back door past sequence-level convergence; neither admission route ties its evidence to the source result
findings.description: The core boundary that is supposed to stop a single usable solve from certifying its own numerical adequacy only checks a report object the caller hands over. That report is never linked to the source result. (1) AdmissibleAnalyticPrediction.validation is a separate field and is never compared with source_result.validation. Nothing asks whether the model is actually closed-form: not the solver, not the convergence state, not the model. So an iterative numerical solve (convergence=CONVERGED, whose own report claims NUMERICALLY_CONVERGED) is admitted as 'analytic' if the caller attaches any report that only reaches DIMENSIONALLY_VALID. The 'routes are disjoint' refusal (claims NUMERICALLY_CONVERGED -> refuse) fires only when the passed report would have cleared the numerical route anyway. A numerical source that never established convergence is exactly the case that gets through. (2) The numerical route accepts the source's own single-solve report as `sequence_validation`. Nothing checks that the report describes a sequence, this model or these observables. (3) A source result with no models, no solver and no validity crosses either route: _require_applicability_not_refuted iterates over result.models, which is empty. binding_ref and verification_ref are free strings that are never checked against provenance. (4) Downstream, AdmittedForwardRow accepts both routes identically. admission_route appears only as a prefix of an admission_refs string that nothing parses, so a posterior cannot tell which evidence backs a row.

1. No production path reaches it. A domain adapter would have to pick the analytic type for a discretized model and write an analytic_basis for it, which is a false declaration.
2. The numerical route is equally caller-trusted by design. NUMERICALLY_CONVERGED needs no issuer (_issuer_gap covers only the three external levels), so a one-line hand-built check gets a solve with no convergence evidence admitted. The analytic route gives a deliberate caller nothing extra. What it does add is a quiet path for a new adapter that makes an honest-looking mistake.
3. Downstream results are identical either way: the posterior weights come out the same whichever route admitted the rows.
4. Point 2, the numerical route accepting the source's own single-solve report, is weaker than claimed. CSTR and conduction1d do not claim NUMERICALLY_CONVERGED on a single solve, so their own report is refused. Only a domain that awards that level per solve (electrical/dc does) would pass, and what that level means is the domain's decision.

Net: the guard is silently weaker than the class presents it, and a cheap core check (require convergence NOT_APPLICABLE or no solver, and validation being source_result.validation) is missing. That is P2.

findings.title: Spread-like quantities on offset temperature scales convert as absolute values: a degC tolerance or sigma on a kelvin quantity becomes ~274 K, while the correct delta_degC form crashes
findings.description: Quantity makes no distinction between absolute values and differences. Every generic core field that is really a difference (ConstraintDefinition.tolerance, the margin it reports, GaussianObservation.sigma) is converted with the absolute Quantity.to. Declaring a '2 degC' tolerance on a kelvin bound yields a 275.15 K tolerance, so a 600 K reading passes a 358.15 K limit. A '0.5 degC' sigma on a kelvin reading yields 273.65 K, so a 50 K misfit has chi2 0.033 instead of 10000 and any goodness-of-fit or near-duplicate test on it is meaningless. The physically correct declaration, a delta_degC tolerance or sigma on a degC value, passes require_same_dimension and then raises pint's DimensionalityError, which is not a UnitCompatibilityError or ScientificCoreError. So the core refuses the right spelling with an untyped crash and silently accepts the wrong one. The reported margin is stored in the bound's offset unit (10 degC), and any consumer converting it gets 283.15 K. Domains guard their own spans (_require_ratio_scale, the excursion-bound checks), but the generic core types have no such guard, although is_ratio_scale exists in the same module.
findings.evidence: constraints.py:127-135 (tolerance.to(bound.units) with only a sign check); constraints.py:147-152 and 181-186 (tol and margin in bound units); grid.py:63-65 (sigma.magnitude_in(value.units)); grid.py:117-120 (numeric_vectors); split.py:104-107 and 443-445 (same sigma conversion before the difference trick); quantity.py:872-915 (Quantity.to has no difference semantics). repro_offset_spreads.py output: "effective tolerance in bound unit: 275.15 kelvin" / "600 K <= 358.15 K (+'2 degC' tol): satisfied margin 33.299999999999955 kelvin" / "300 degC <= 85 degC (+'2 degC' tol): satisfied" / "== 300 K +/- '1 degC' at 500 K: True" / "margin of 75 degC under 85 degC: 10.0 degree_Celsius -> a consumer converting to K reads 283.15 kelvin" / "observation sigma as used by the likelihood: 273.65 kelvin". repro_sigma_delta.py: "degC value + 0.5 delta_degC sigma (the correct declaration) raises pint.errors.DimensionalityError" / "K value + '0.5 degC' sigma: sigma used = 273.65 K; chi2 of a 50 K misfit = 0.0334 (true sigma 0.5 K gives 10000)". repro_quantity_p3.py: "ConstraintDefinition(bound 85 degC, tolerance 2 delta_degC) raises pint.errors.DimensionalityError".

findings.fix_direction: Give the core a difference conversion: convert as (value + spread) - value, or require is_ratio_scale on the spread's unit, and map delta units onto the value's scale. In ConstraintDefinition and GaussianObservation, refuse a spread declared on an offset unit unless it is the same unit as the value it spreads, and accept delta units. Record the margin in a ratio-scale (delta) unit. Wrap pint conversion errors in UnitCompatibilityError inside Quantity.to.

I reproduced the finding at 294c129, with engcore importing from src. ConstraintDefinition converts its tolerance with the plain absolute conversion Quantity.to(bound.units), guarded only by require_same_dimension and a sign check. GaussianObservation.__post_init__ and ObservationSet.numeric_vectors convert sigma with sigma.magnitude_in(value.units). split.observation_content_digest and _base_value_and_sigma make the same absolute conversion before their difference step, despite the comment saying sigma is handled as a difference.

- Kelvin spreads on degC values are refused with misleading messages ('must be non-negative', 'strictly positive').
- The split digest treats a 0.5 degC sigma and a 273.65 K sigma as identical content.

The margin reported in degC (10 degC) does read 283.15 K if a consumer converts it absolutely, as claimed.

The audit document never mentions offset units, so this is new.

I lowered the severity from P1 to P2:
- The silent wrong result needs a spread declared in an offset unit that differs from the value's unit.
- Nothing in the package calls ConstraintDefinition.check.
- The in-package GaussianObservation producers use ohm, not temperature.
- The MCP boundary does not accept constraints.

The mechanism is real and I reproduced it against src. The core has no separate type for a difference: ConstraintDefinition's tolerance (constraints.py:133 and :147-151) and GaussianObservation's sigma (grid.py:64 and :117-119, split.py:106 and :445) are converted with Quantity.to, which treats every temperature as an absolute reading.

What happens depends on the unit pairing:

- **degC value or bound with a delta_degC spread:** refused with pint's untyped DimensionalityError, which is not a ScientificCoreError.
- **degC value or bound with a kelvin spread:** also refused, with a misleading typed message ("tolerance must be non-negative" / "sigma must be strictly positive").
- **Matching units (degC with degC, kelvin with kelvin or delta_degC):** handled correctly.

Both key cases are reachable. I built a grid end to end: a model misfit that the CORE-001 goodness-of-fit gate refuses at 0.5 kelvin or 0.5 delta_degC passes silently (verdict None) when the sigma is declared as '0.5 degC'. That silently turns off one of the new fixes. The finding is new; the audit document never mentions offset or degC units.

1. No runtime path reaches it. ConstraintDefinition.check is never called in src, and the margin is only serialized. MCP and the studies never build temperature observations (tcr uses ohm, K2/K3 are not temperature).
2. It needs a caller to pair a kelvin value with a spread written in degC, which pint by definition reads as an absolute temperature.
3. On the sigma side, the posterior and prediction widths get wider, not narrower. The false confidence is only in model adequacy, because the goodness-of-fit gate stays silent.

The same pattern very likely affects observation_sigma in uq/predictive.py:69 and hybrid_uq/predictive.py:346/465; I did not run those.

findings.title: Experiment.best counts a candidate as feasible when any constraint check it carries passed: declared constraints need not be checked, and checks are not tied to their numbers or the result
findings.description: CORE-015 is recorded as FIXED: 'Experiment.best ranks only candidates whose models were all assessed IN_DOMAIN, with declared constraints checked and satisfied'. The code filters on e.is_feasible, which is all(check.satisfied) over whatever ConstraintCheck records the evaluation carries. Nothing requires one check per declared constraint. A check naming an undeclared constraint counts. ConstraintCheck is a free record: satisfied is not reconciled with margin (satisfied=True with margin -2.5 A is accepted and survives a round trip). Its value is not compared with the result's metric, and nothing names the bound. An evaluation whose result carries T_hot=900 K against a declared 400 K ceiling and response 3 A against a declared 0.5 A ceiling is ranked best, because its only check is a forged satisfied check on an undeclared name. A second evaluation that checked only one of two declared constraints also counts as feasible.

The finding holds; I could not refute it. `is_feasible` (evaluation.py:167-172) only asks whether every check the evaluation happens to carry is satisfied. `best` (experiment.py:201-207) accepts `is_feasible is True`, and nothing on the path compares the check names against `self.constraints`. findings.title: Consensus relative difference is taken on offset-scale magnitudes: the verdict depends on route order and unit, and a false CROSS_SOLVER_VALIDATED is possible
findings.description: The CORE-018 fix converts each name into 'the unit of the first declared route that reports it'. It then scores |a-b|/max(|a|,|b|) on those magnitudes, which is meaningful only on a ratio scale. For a temperature, the same pair of results gets a different verdict depending on which route is declared first: degC-first gives rel 3.7e-9 against tol 1e-9 and no level, K-first gives rel 3.3e-10 and CROSS_SOLVER_VALIDATED. When both routes report in degC near absolute zero, a true 1e-8 relative disagreement scores 3.7e-11 and is awarded CROSS_SOLVER_VALIDATED, while the same numbers in kelvin are refused. At room temperature in degC, justified agreement is refused. The fix introduced the route-order dependence, and the same-unit case was never gated: is_ratio_scale exists but consensus does not use it. The CORE-014 operating-point rule (oracles._same_operating_point, used by ScientificResult) has the same pattern: 0.02 degC vs 0.020000001 degC are 'different operating points', while the identical 1e-9 K difference in kelvin is 'the same'.
